claims.text: As-processed HfNbTiVAl10 has a hierarchical heterostructure with multilevel chemical fluctuations and spatial heterogeneities.
A multi-fidelity surrogate combining reduced-order FE, localized high-fidelity FE, and machine-learning regression can predict Young’s modulus, yield strength, and fracture toughness in HfNbTiVAl10.
Low-fidelity FE simulations on representative volume elements can capture the alloy’s global stress–strain response.
Localized high-fidelity FE analyses can characterize critical crack-initiation and crack-propagation regions.
The model would be calibrated with low- and high-fidelity FE outputs plus selected nanoindentation, tensile, and fracture measurements obtained under controlled room-temperature conditions.

Stress-concentration descriptors, statistical measures of chemical fluctuations, and localized crack-tip results mediate the relationship between hierarchical microstructure and macroscopic mechanical response.
Low-fidelity FE provides rapid approximations of global stress fields and mechanical responses caused by heterogeneities.
Machine-learning regression can map FE-derived descriptors to macroscopic mechanical properties.
Adding localized high-fidelity crack-region analyses improves fracture-toughness prediction by capturing microscale phenomena missed by low-fidelity simulations.
The integrated model will predict Young’s modulus with an error within ±5–7%.
The integrated model will predict yield strength with an error within ±5–7%.
The integrated model will predict fracture toughness with an error within ±5–7%.
The proposed method will reduce computational cost by nearly two orders of magnitude relative to full-scale CALPHAD or first-principles simulations.
Full-scale ab initio and CALPHAD methods are computationally intensive for this prediction task.
Conventional machine-learning approaches are less effective at capturing the complex fracture mechanisms of hierarchical heterostructures.
The method becomes unreliable when FE representations omit important microstructural heterogeneities or localized analyses omit emergent crack mechanisms.
Extreme loading, unforeseen temperature variation, or microstructural scales beyond FE resolution can make the model unreliable.
Prediction performance depends on FE calibration precision, selection of representative crack regions, and the quality and consistency of validation data.
Localized high-fidelity analyses should reduce the variance of toughness predictions relative to a low-fidelity-only model.
A prospective blinded comparison against standardized tensile and fracture measurements can test the model without exposing it to the target experimental results.
